Did I just beat TypeSafe AI's Jev on calibration with an 11-second TF-IDF baseline ?!

Here is what happened: my 151M model initially scored 26.10% on LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions (400 cases, 2,000 decisions). Uniform random chance on that split is 29.85%.

Before touching model weights, i audited the evaluation harness and caught three bugs:

Appended __insufficient_evidence__ to every schema on a benchmark with zero ground-truth abstentions.
Dropped criteria on binary Noul queries, predicting "true" 100% of the time.
Appended (Value: X) to score levels, breaking label matching.
To establish an honest reference floor, we trained character 3-6 n-gram TF-IDF + Logistic Regression on the 1,200 training cases. It ran in 11 seconds on a CPU.

Here is where the 11-second baseline beat Jev:

Calibration error across all workflows (ECE, lower is better):
Overall: 0.0207 (vs Jev 0.1440)
Security Incidents: 0.0238
Invoice Processing: 0.0290

Customer Service accuracy:
TF-IDF hit 69.00% accuracy, clearing Jev's reported 68% overall benchmark average on CPU text statistics alone.

Binary Noul judgments:
75.83% accuracy with 0.0464 ECE, proving that binary decision criteria do not need billion-parameter attention to calibrate.

Why did classical ML win on calibration?

Logistic Regression directly optimizes convex Bernoulli log-loss against empirical class frequencies. Its predicted probabilities naturally match empirical hit rates across every confidence bin without teacher-distillation distortion or post-hoc temperature hacks.
Clean wiring and empirical reference floors matter more than pretraining compute.

Full breakdown, benchmark logs, and reproducible script are live on GitHub: link in comment

q.t:
TypeSafe AI came out of stealth with Jev, and access is behind a waitlist.

I built an open source version Verdict (Open-jev) you can run right now in a browser tab: And its a real post trained model..(link in comments)

It is a post trained 151M parameters model. ModernBERT-base with a GLiClass head. Instead of token-by-token autoregressive decoding or JSON string parsing, it takes an input text and candidate options, then returns calibrated probabilities and an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome in a single forward pass.

Some of The numbers:

Calibration: 0.83% adaptive expected calibration error on 1,000 held-out cases. I trained with a multi-class Brier score term, then tried standard post-hoc temperature scaling. Temperature scaling degraded the metrics, so the model ships with temperature 1.0.

Order invariance: reversing the option list flips 3.0% of predictions across 1,000 cases. For reference, another open Jev reproduction measured a frozen Qwen3.5-4B at 27.8% flips on the same perturbation, though on their own 36-case fixture rather than mine. Full bidirectional attention evaluates the candidate list simultaneously instead of scanning left to right.

Shuffled-context control: Pairing questions with the wrong document drops accuracy from 95.0% to 22.4% and drives abstention from 21.8% to 72.7%, confirming the model actively conditions on the context.

Latency: 89ms median in-browser via WebGPU, and 35.6ms via ONNX on CPU at 5 candidates.

The negative results:

I ran 12 use cases on public data across both checkpoints and three label framings three passed the promotion gate. Passage re-ranking hit 11.9%, jailbreak screening 34.9%, and phishing detection 57.5%. 

On 337 cases from TypeSafe's public evaluation set, Jev reaches 90.8%, a 26B diffusion model reaches 88.4%, and Verdict reaches 48.1%.which is expected since its just 151M param model but working on trying it on bigger scale as well.

A 151M encoder is calibrated, order-invariant, and fast, but it lacks broad world knowledge. 

In a tiered architecture where a cheap model gates an expensive one, knowing exact failure boundaries is essential. 48 of the 50 classification errors fall below a 0.95 confidence threshold, making the gate predictable.

For the next steps i will be testing the same harness on a larger backbone a bigger model with more params to see whether order invariance holds at scale or depends strictly on bidirectional attention.

Small demo built with @typesafeai Jev and @cactuscompute Needle

Coding by @claudeai Fable, maps by @openstreetmap, additional information by @mapillary, voices by @Alibaba_Qwen Qwen3 TTS, and music - which I did not ask for, btw - by @StepFun_ai  ACE-Step 1.5

Three prompts total.

"dude, I have no idea what we are going to do here... but 1) not a kortexa repo yet, so no factory, pure vibing, 2) grab keys from <redacted> if/when need, 3) I want us to figure out something cool with OpenStreetMap and/or Mappilary and Typesafe Jev."

"also, if you can figure out how to fit Cactus Needle from needle.server into this, more power to you."

"do a local app - I don't care if node.js or python/fastapi for server, and cool web client, once it's up and running, use the "impeccable polish" skill to make the UX look cool, then do a short demo video and drop it on my desktop. you can use tts.server on <redacted> for narration with Archibal's voice or if you want to make it a dialog, use Archibald and Mira voices. :-)
I am off to bed, because tomorrow sleep... and maybe work for bread and tokens."
tr: Archibald, meet Mappity. It's a map you can just talk to. A talking map? Marvelous. Does it also do my taxes? Watch, my kid is melting down and needs sugar. Immediately. Every place you see just answered with a probability. 400 judgments, about a second, a fraction of a cent. 400 opinions in one second, like my family, but useful. On the left, Needle, a tiny local model, thought sugar was a landmark. Jev gave that one percent. Overruled. They mark each other's homework, I approve. Next, cozy coffee, within five minutes' walk of the aquarium. Needle pulls out the aquarium, and the five minutes. Code does the geography, Jev decides what cozy means. One that no category can answer. Somewhere I'd feel fine walking to, alone, at 11 at night. Jev decided the street matters, so we asked Mappillary what its cameras saw. Each place is judged twice, itself and its street, and code multiplies the two. So those little specs are actual lamp posts, good heavens. Very worthy, but can it do anything frivolous? Let's play a guessing game. It's now thinking of one of these 60 places. Can I eat there? I only hear one answer. But every place answered, so the odds shift across the whole map. Does it serve alcohol? Bayes theorem, as a pub quiz. Stand back, I shall guess. I demand a recount. Open street map, Mappillary, type safe Jev, and cactus Needle. About a second per question. No chat bot anywhere. Splendid. Now ask it where one finds a decent cup of tea.

t:
Ok I was busy doing actual work today, but here is another Jev experiment ... Code linting, for specifically the kind of "anti-patterns" that LLMs tend to include, "inline" as part of the code gen. process giving immediate feedback.

The idea here is that while you can create a set of ast/ or other programmatic rules for alot of these, the models tend to get really creative to satisfy the linter but still sneak in the "issue" in the code. You already know I'll say it, Goodhart's law!

But here the judgement can draw on the broader heuristics of large-ish model but obviously for cheaper and near instant compared to using another LLM. So this allow to use Jev in the tool call loop directly and mitigate the issues in the current set of changes causing issues in down stream code gen. 

Kinda like the '80 movies where "only a ninja, can kill a ninja" ...

This is obviously just a quick test prototype but you can imagine doing something like this using @opencode plugins (or something like that) to hook into a real harness and its tool calls.

t: Jev tone analysis, with apologies to Helena, Montana.

Early results from my all-nighter experiments with the new (non-LLM, "System One" class) Jev model from @typesafeai 

I ran LLMBar, JudgeBench, and RewardBench comparing Jev (hosted by Typesafe) to LLMs GPT-OSS, Deepseek flash, and GLM flash (hosted by @FireworksAI_HQ)

as you can see, Jev's nearest competitor in these evals (which are designed to be hard, and may be a little too tough for both) is GPT-OSS.

GPT-OSS has higher quality on most tests across the board (but lower on the easiest one, LLMBar), at "only" 5-6x the price of Jev.  it's also ~15x slower.

GLM and Qwen are 50-100x more expensive for similar quality scores on the easiest one.

I think Jev is going to find its way into a _LOT_ of production workloads beyond evals... but evals alone would give it a pretty freaking large market.

I'm salivating and I can't wait for it to be enterprise ready!

【主な機能】

q.t:
There has been a lot of talk around Jev as a next gen 'model', which cannot be far from reality.

Let me try and explain with an analogy of airport:

LLM = the pilot.
It can reason about a complex situation, make a plan, communicate, adapt, write things, use tools, and solve novel problems.

Jev = the air-traffic control system around the pilot.
It constantly makes small decisions:
Which runway?
Is this request risky?
Which model should handle this?
Is confidence high enough to continue?
Does this need escalation?
Did the previous step succeed?

You wouldn't replace the pilot with air-traffic control.

And you wouldn't want the pilot personally answering 10,000 little routing questions every second either.

Very exciting that we have a new infrastructure to make LLMs more reliable and consistent.

tr: Here we have a demo of using the TypeSafe API to create a smart home assistant. We're able to issue commands to the smart home and using only TypeSafe to evaluate what should be done on the devices in the home. So we can do turn off all of the lights and over here in our mock smart home we can see that all the lights turned off. We can say turn on the living room lights and those turned on. We can say shut off all the music in the house and the smart speaker turned off, get the coffee boiling and the coffee maker turns on. So on the right side here we have the full trace of exactly what's happening on every call. So we just did get the coffee boiling. So let's look at how we actually made that decision. We're actually only calling the TypeSafe API one time in all of these requests but we are supplying a whole bunch of prompts in that one call to the API with everything that we need to make the evaluation for a multitude of different commands. So in this particular case we're using a choice primitive to decide what is the user's intent. So is it a smart home command? Is it an information request or is it a smart home query like asking the status of a device? In this case it's a smart home command. We determine that it is not a compound request so it does not contain multiple commands in one. We do that with a new primitive. We say what is the scope of the request in the case of the coffee maker? It was a specific device. What kind of device is being targeted? It's an appliance. Which specific device should receive the command is the kitchen coffee maker? And then finally what should happen to the appliances which is turn on? So we're turning on the kitchen coffee maker and that becomes the one action. But what's notable here is that in that same call to the type safe API we also asked other questions like what should happen to the fans? What should happen to the locks? What should happen to the speakers? But our code didn't even look at the responses to those because we already know we're targeting a specific device. It's an appliance. It's the kitchen coffee maker. So this is an example of speculative prompting. So we asked what should happen to the locks and the type safe API returned a bit of an unknown response like it's got 79% likely unlocked 21% likely lock. It makes sense that it's not certain about it because the command didn't have anything to do with locks at all. But we ask it anyway because in the case that it did have to do with locks, we're going to have that answer already available in our code without having to do another round trip. So if I say lock up the whole house in this example, what should happen to the locks becomes pertinent and the what should happen to the appliances is not pertinent. So in this case of locking up the whole house we can see it was also a smart home command. The scope was the whole house and the kind of device being targeted was a lock. This shows that by leveraging the fact that type safe returns very, very quickly and very inexpensively when you cram as many prompts as you need into a single API call, you can get the advantage of getting all of the intelligence back at once and relying on your code to branch where you want. But let's get into a couple other patterns that we show in this example. So here is turn off the kitchen lights and lock the office door. This is a compound request. In this particular case, we're doing something a little bit trickier. We got to scroll up a bit more to see here. So one of the earliest things that we evaluate is does this request contain multiple commands and it does 98% probabilities. So yes, it absolutely does. We're asking about the kitchen lights and locking the office door, which we can already see it did it correctly. This is a case where we're using the strength of type safes very, very fast primitives pairing with a traditional LLM when actual text extraction is needed when text generation is needed. So as soon as we determine that this request contains multiple commands, we decide to kick it out to an LLM to say split this into the discrete sub commands. And the LLM returned one is to turn off the kitchen lights and two is to lock the office door. And then we're running each of those against the same logic that we run all of our commands. So we can see up top at the timing here, we have the type safe API returned in 178 milliseconds, we then called Claude Haiku to just get as quick as possible to get the split into two commands. And then we did two parallel requests to type safe for each of those two split commands. And now we were able to fully evaluate the answer. And then finally, the other pattern that we have here is showing how if we ask who won the World Series in 1989, we are just looking for a general intelligence question is the kind of thing that you would want an LLM to answer. We can put type safe as the first has the responsibility to look at the response immediately very, very quickly determine where to

q.t:
Spent an hour on YT livestream today with the Jev model via the typesafe API. Thanks to typesafe team for helping out with credits.

The main use-case for this LM is to predict context aware decisions when the decision space of the problem is known apriori.

The biggest downside is that you CANNOT generate new tokens - it only works as a classifier + confidence-predictor. You cannot use it even for extraction or form-filling stuff. You always have to pass in a list of candidate answers as well.

IOW, you must programmatically create a candidate list BEFORE calling the API - and the model will output the probabilities for each entry given the context. You can send few shot examples and instructions too... dspy-style... but the output schema is fixed into 3 types of things: Choice (enums), Noul (boolean+probability), and Score (ordered value)

We also went into masked LM and parallel constrained decoding. We discussed theories about how the model functions - and how it happens so quickly.

Random thought: I feel like the next version of this model is probably going to be running small autoregressive/diffusion heads over the output token embeddings. This way prefill can still remain parallel, but arbitrary token output is also possible.

q.t:
12M+ views so I had to dig into this

Is it just a hyped launch or something novel and actually useful?

I’m leaning to the latter and will break it down with a practical example

First, understand that Jev isn’t a typical LLM that you prompt and get back a written response

It’s much more specific - you give Jev context along with a set of questions and possible answers and it returns probabilities to each question and answer set, and it does it super fast and cheap

I found it helpful to think through a simple example:

Let’s say you’re an online retailer and you get hundreds of inquiries a day

You put an agent in the workflow that looks at each inquiry and makes a judgement call on the next action and then generates a response

But that LLM judgement call can be messy - LLMs still have a tendency to make shit up or respond in ways that you don’t like, so we put humans in the loop

What Jev does is look at each inquiry and makes a fast decision on the nature of it so the workflow can take the next best action with confidence

It doesn’t replace the workflow or the LLM entirely, it handles the fuzzy fork in the road that used to require a human to read the message first

Let’s say you get a customer email:

“This jacket sucks! The zipper jammed the first time I wore it and now it won’t close so I want my money back.”

That message lands in the retailer’s system along with a few facts the company already has: the order is 11 days old, the return window is 30 days, the jacket was $100, and this customer has one previous order with no refunds

In a typical LLM workflow you’d let the model decide what to do and have it initiate that action and send a reply email, BUT many companies want a HITL in many of these cases, especially ones where it’s not entirely clear what to do

Imagine the LLM replies to the email with troubleshooting instructions on how to fix the zipper - probably not the best action

With Jev, the company doesn’t ask it to write a reply, it asks a few specific questions about the email and order

>Does the customer want a refund?
>What is the main issue: defective product, didn’t like it, late delivery, or something else?
>How unhappy does the person sound?
>Does this look like it falls inside the published return policy?
>Should this go to returns, quality control, or a human agent?

Jev looks at the email and the order context, then answers all of those at the same time with a probability score - no prose, just a score

In this case the picture comes back fairly clear: yes, this is a refund request, the issue is a defective product, frustration is high but not explosive, the request is inside the return window, returns should own it

That is enough for the retailer’s existing rules to take the next action with confidence 

If Jev had been less sure - say the email was sarcastic, the order was 45 days old, or it was unclear whether the customer wanted a refund or a replacement - the workflow could put the ticket in a human queue instead of guessing

The useful part is the handoff, specifically knowing when to pass it to the next step in a workflow or route to HITL

If Claude were the judge in a less clear situation, you’re likely to get a long winded answer that still leaves you wondering what to do next, and it would have taken longer and cost a lot more

This was a simple example but I can see how this can be incredibly useful in complex enterprise workflows which is why I lean towards novel and useful over just a hyped new thing

Will be following this one closely

q.t:
I just open sourced Foreman: a software factory foreman built with @typesafeai's Jev.

Coding agents work the factory floor. Foreman watches them, continuously assessing progress, completeness, tests, drift, and verification, and intervenes when needed.

GitHub: https://github.com/thruwire/foreman

tr: Alright, so we're really excited about JEV. Today we released Foreman, which is an open source project. Foreman is basically a supervisor for coding agents. You give it a software task, and Codex does the engineering. While Codex works, Foreman watches its output, code changes, and recent attempts. A fast model, in this case, JEV asks, "Is it making progress? Is it stock? Are the requirements satisfied?" A Python policy then decides whether to keep going, retry, ask for help, or start an independent verification pass when the evidence calls for it. The key is that Foreman can make those calls while Codex is still working. Codex chooses how to write code, Foreman watches the overall job. Every assessment and intervention goes into an event timeline, so you can see what Foreman saw and why it acted. It's early, we'd love your feedback, but it shows how coding agents could be easier to direct and inspect.

q.t:
this is the easiest way to understand Jev:

LLMs generate answers.

Jev makes decisions.

that sounds like a small difference, but it actually changes the entire use case.

say you give a normal LLM this:

“here’s a user, their account history, payment behavior, support chats, device data, etc.

tell me if this looks risky.”

the LLM might reason through it and return:

“yes, this looks high risk.”

maybe in JSON if you ask nicely.

with Jev, you define the possible decisions upfront:

risk:

* low
* medium
* high

manual review:

* yes
* no

and Jev returns something closer to:

risk = high (96%)
manual review = yes (91%)

that’s basically the product.

it’s not trying to be another ChatGPT.

it’s more like an AI-native if statement.

instead of:

if transaction > $10,000:
review()

you can start thinking more like:

if “does this behavior look suspicious?” > 95%:
review()

and that opens up a pretty interesting category of software.

a few assumptions I had at first that turned out to be wrong:

1. “so it’s just a classifier?”

kind of, but that undersells it.

the input can be messy real-world context, and you can ask multiple typed questions about that state at once.

fraud?
churn?
escalate?
eligible?
priority?

all from the same input.

2. “so it replaces GPT / Claude?”

not really.

I actually think the interesting architecture is:

Jev decides WHAT needs to happen

Claude / GPT reason or generate WHEN deeper intelligence is needed

normal code executes the deterministic stuff.

Jev becomes the routing layer.

3. “it can’t hallucinate?”

this one needs nuance.

if your allowed answers are:

LOW
MEDIUM
HIGH

Jev won’t suddenly invent:

“EXTREMELY HIGH 🚨”

the output structure is constrained.

but it can still be wrong.

HIGH at 92% can still be the wrong decision.

so “no hallucinations” doesn’t mean “always correct.”

4. “why not just force an LLM to return JSON?”

you can.

we already do this everywhere.

but you still deal with generation latency, schema validation, retries, weird outputs, confidence estimation and a lot of glue code.

Jev is designed around the decision itself rather than text generation.

5. “why should I care?”

because most software is ultimately a giant tree of:

if this → do that
if this → route here
if this → escalate
if this → reject
if this → ask a human

Jev is basically asking:

what if those if statements could understand messy human context?

that’s a much more interesting framing than “another AI model.”

I can see this being very useful for:

fraud / risk
support routing
moderation
PR / QA automation
lead scoring
compliance
workflow orchestration
agent routing

especially as the cheap + fast decision layer sitting in front of larger reasoning models.

early tech, obviously.

but the category itself makes a lot of sense.

t:
As the discussion here continues, there are three areas where System One models like Jev are particularly interesting:

- Continuous evals and monitoring
- How it supports long-horizon agents through custom verifiers
- Recursive self-improving agent harness

It's not just about affordability. Models that specialize in decision-making, like Jev, are ideal primitives for enabling more effective use of frontier agents.

The same philosophy goes here: not everything requires a frontier model.

In 2021, I trained and published a specialized character based deep neural network to classify scientification publications, trained on 25 000 000 abstracts, we stop because it was not improving anymore.

ONLY 5 years later! That work is completely replaced by Jev and Qwen 27b.

Jev is essentially a classifier of anything. this can be very very convenient!
Imagine how much money typesafeAI made with the jev launch. Like it must be double digits at this point already

没有人能100%地说出Jev是什么

除非他们发布一份技术论文，否则我们只是在猜测

人们把Jev说成一个编码器（类似bert）/分类器，并说“它不是LLM”，就像他们认为只有解码器的模型是唯一的LLM一样！

非自回归解码器才是一个有趣的猜测，它将尝试并行生成许多或所有输出令牌

它可以是语言模型的一部分

q.t:
Encoder 的卷土重来

BERT 本来是一条极有潜力的路线：高效地把输入压成 representation。但它停留在了 task-specific 时代，每个任务都需要微调。

GPT 早期同样如此，后来却沿着 scaling、in-context learning 和 instruction tuning 走向了 泛化，把自然语言变成 universal task interface。分类、判断、推理、工具调用，统统变成 generation。

于是 decoder-only 赢下了整个 paradigm，encoder 也失去了继续探索 general classifier 和 general representation model 的历史机会。

但 Agent 改变了 workload。模型开始面对越来越大的输入、越来越重的 KV cache、越来越频繁的循环调用，此时，用一个巨大的 decoder 完整 prefill，再 autoregressive decode 几个 token 来完成一次判断，开始显得昂贵。

Jev 恰好等到了这个窗口。它试图补上 BERT 当年没有走完的路线，保留 GPT 的 task generalization，同时重新获得 encoder 和 classifier 式的 decision efficiency，成为面向 service、面向 Agent 的 泛化 decision model。

Not to mention you also get probabilities from Jev, which are quite well-calibrated (expected calibration error is 1.74 percentage points averaged across benches - its 0.26pp at best and 6.96pp at worst)

t:
网一断，用户第一反应是去推特骂客服

那么问题来了：能不能在品牌自己承认故障之前，就从这些推文里看出来？

我们拿 2017 年七个品牌客服号的 170,400 条推文试了一次，Spectrum、Comcast、Hulu、动视、Cox、Sprint、Verizon

每条推文让 TypeSafe Jev 回答两个问题：这条在说什么，问题是不是大面积的。全部打完 1.84 美元

01｜标准答案，用品牌自己的话

客服回复里第一次说出"你所在区域有故障""我们已知并在排查"，就算品牌承认了。泛泛的"请私信我们"不算，否认的不算

人工抽查 40 条，37 条判得对

一共找出 62 次故障。其中 Comcast 唯一的一次，正好是 2017 年 11 月 6 日的全美断网

02｜同样的误报预算下，Jev 抓得更多也更早

每个信号都调到每周约 1.8 次误报

Jev 的"服务挂了 × 大面积"：抓到 17 次，比品牌早 4.1 小时
只看推文总量：10 次，早 2.4 小时
关键词清单：12 次，早 1.7 小时
情绪分析：9 次，垫底

三档误报预算下，Jev 抓到的都比推文总量多，最宽松那档 p = 0.007

03｜但一份好的关键词清单差不多够用

报故障的人用词很集中：挂了、没网、有人也这样吗。Jev 能多抓到"我的 wifi 今天搞什么鬼"这种，但对关键词的领先在统计上始终不显著

和上一篇 issue 流实验放在一起看：维护者一天内就修好时，什么信号都来不及；组织反应比用户慢时，Jev 过滤后的推文流能提前几个小时

数据集没有明确许可，又是别人的推文，仓库里只放了推文编号、时间和 Jev 的回答

JEV TIP 004:

Turn failure into skill improvements by adding an incident field to your agent’s completion report.

Send the incident report and active skill to JEV against explicit gap criteria.

If it qualifies, revise or create a skill and then replay incidents as evals before promotion.

q.t:
JEV TIP 003:

When an agent marks an attempt as failed, send JEV:

> task contract
> failure report
> failed strategy
> proposed retry strategy
> criteria for what counts as a legitimate retry

If the retry doesn’t meet the criteria, force a replan, escalate, or stop.

The pipeline was:

1. Summarize each paper with DeepSeek V4 Flash
2. Send the title + summary + 24 possible topics to Jev
3. Use Jev to classify each paper
4. Visualize everything on http://1kpapers.com

The summaries cost $3.99 on @togethercompute. The classifications cost $0.08 on @typesafeai.

So for just over $4 of inference, I ended up with a pretty useful way to explore the top AI research papers from the past year.

I think this is where things are heading: different models for different parts of the workflow, instead of using one model for everything.

I’m running evals on the Jev classifications before replacing the current ones, but the site is already live: http://1kpapers.com

とりあえず Jev がどういう問題クラスに対して、どれくらいのインプットまで適切に回答できるかを検証。
(Size rank については2枚目)
Parity が 8bit ですら低すぎるのが気になる。

① Lookup：ビット列の、指定した位置が1か。
② Majority：ビット列の中で1が0より多いか。
③ Parity：ビット列に含まれる1の個数が奇数か。
④ Product bit：二進数で与えた2整数を掛け算し、積の指定した桁が1か。
⑤ S5 composition：5個のラベルの並べ替えを順に適用し、すべて元の位置に戻るか。
⑥ Boolean formula：真・偽をAND／ORで組み合わせた式が、最終的に真になるか。
⑦ Undirected reach：無向グラフで、始点から終点へたどり着けるか。
⑧ Directed reach：有向グラフで、始点から終点へたどり着けるか。
⑨ Circuit value：0と1をAND／OR／XORで順に計算し、途中の結果も再利用する回路で、最終出力が1か。

Credit assignment in AI matters.

Jev is receiving attention for schema-defined probabilistic decisions. But the underlying capability, schema-conditioned multi-task classification in is not new.

At @fastinoAI we built #GLiNER2 and released it publicly in 2025, published at #EMNLP2025: one text input, user-defined label spaces, multiple classification tasks, and confidence scores, all in one forward pass.

It has been open source under Apache-2.0 since then, and the ecosystem reflects that, with multiple fine-tunes across Hugging Face.

The framing is compelling, and Jev is heavily optimized for classification, so it may well be stronger on that specific task. But GLiNER2 is more general. Beyond classification it handles entities, structured extraction, and relations, which is what let us ship domain models on the same interface:

Guardrails (GLiGuard): https://huggingface.co/fastino/gliguard-LLMGuardrails-300M
PII detection and masking: https://huggingface.co/fastino/gliner2-privacy-filter-PII-multi

Paper: https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-demos.10/
Code: https://github.com/fastino-ai/GLiNER2
HF: https://huggingface.co/collections/fastino/gliner25-models

tr: I'm Diego Almeida, founder of Typesafe AI, and at OpenAI, I co-created ChatGBT and RLHF, the post-training algorithm behind most frontier AI. Our team trained the first models to be superhuman at instruction following, what we now call Chat. And we asked ourselves, are models that are superhuman at Chat AGI? The answer was obviously not, but the trillion dollar question is why not? RLHF has led to LMs that are optimizing for human preferences and include issues such as mode dropping, overconfidence, and an overall lack of reliability. These flaws mean that LMs require humans in the loop, and almost no true automation can be done. At Typesafe, we've spent two years building in stealth, and we're finally ready to share our new type of foundation model that's optimized for automation. System 1 models. With a new architecture, new sampler, and new training algorithm, reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions. Movements are clear if you see them side by side. Ask a System 1 model a ton of structured questions, just like you would an LM. Get the answers back near instantly. Meanwhile, LMs take hundreds of times longer to finish responding. Look at how the LM generates sequentially, which is great for a natural conversation, but totally useless for computers. LMs extract intelligence from the tiny straw of auto regression, and similar to the jump that transformers made over RNMs, We are replacing sequential computation with parallel, because that is obviously the future. Our System 1 models output decisions with probabilities and confidence instead of words, and they can't hallucinate. They're a lot more like code, reliable, fast, self-consistent, and Typesafe. This opens up a whole new world of possibilities and applications. Today, we're releasing JIV, the first public System 1 model. It's 100 times faster, so real-time AI is finally possible. This is cheaper with input tokens priced at $42 per billion tokens, and output tokens are free because they're finally too f***ing cheap to meter. JIV is super smart, and its intelligence per dollar is literally off the charts. This is just the beginning. We're excited to see what you build with JIV. As we say at Typesafe, we're building prod, not God. We're waiting seconds for responses or paying for words you never asked for. Side effects may include fewer retries, fewer parsers, fewer broken schemas, and intelligence running inside every software loop. Your software may begin moderating every message, routing every ticket, reviewing every document, and making millions of background decisions that were previously too slow or expensive to automate. Entire software categories may be rewritten in the process. As costs fall, usage may increase dramatically. Ask your developer if your industry is ready.

t:
Some follow-up thoughts on my Jev rant. I've also been curious / looking at zero-shot no training tabular models like Google's TabFM and TabPFN:

- Lots and lots of companies have data sitting in tables that they could use to make predictions. Which customers will leave? Which orders will be late? What is this thing likely to sell for?
- With TabFM / TabPFN, you give it historical examples with known outcomes, and new rows you want predictions for. You don't have to train a new model for each problem. You still need labeled examples, though. 'No training' doesn't mean you can skip having useful data.
- This feels like another way to make ML more accessible. Still some work to get your data ready and check if the predictions are useful, but potentially less work than building and tuning a model yourself.
- You can also wrap this in a tool that an LLM calls. The LLM helps you get the data ready, calls the model, and helps you look at the results. I think this could be pretty useful for companies.
- I'd like to try TabFM / TabPFN, Jev, and something like XGBoost (maybe with help from LLMs for feature selection etc) on the same problem. Give them access to the same information and see how they do. How good are the predictions? How much does it cost? How much work does it take to get something useful?
- I would wager that for a lot of problems where you have good historical tabular data, a tabular model or a classically trained model would work better than Jev. But I haven't tested that yet. Would be fun to try it and post the results.
- And this gets back to my earlier point. LLMs make it much easier to build and test all of this stuff now. You can use one to help build a classical ML model, or call a pretrained model, instead of asking the LLM itself to make every prediction.

It's funny that one outcome of all this interest in LLMs might be companies discovering problems they could have solved with ML years ago. Either way, if it gets them to try things and find something useful, that's good.

q.t:
Yes, classifiers existed. BERT, DeBERTa, GLiNER, fine-tuned heads. Most of them were specialized. Pick the labels, train, ship. Changing the rules at runtime meant another training run.

What we did not have was a general-purpose classifier at Terra / Sonnet 5 level intelligence.

You could fake it by asking an LLM for JSON, but that was slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated.

Jev is that missing piece. Labels defined in code, typed answer plus confidence, no extra LLM call.

Classification is not new. What is new is a general-purpose classifier this intelligent, this fast, and this cheap.

t:
Cua 已经给 Jev 做了一个 computer use 接入预览，叫 jev-use，目前还在未合并的 PR 里。

这次可以具体看到，一个只做结构化决策、不生成文本的模型，怎样参与操作电脑。

Cua Driver 负责读取界面和执行操作。应用代码根据当前状态，先构造一组完整的候选动作，每个动作的目标、参数都在本地准备好，再交给 Jev 选择。

Jev 只返回其中一个候选 ID。代码检查这个 ID，再取出本地对应的动作执行。它不能临时编一个工具名、坐标或者一段代码，让 Driver 照着运行。

从模型任务看，就是根据当前观察和目标，对一组候选动作做选择。它尝试降低的是每一步决策的开销，应用代码则明确限定了模型可以选择的范围。

这个分工也意味着，Jev 可以换成别的模型。Cua 没把 TypeSafe 的 SDK、凭据和请求逻辑塞进 Driver，接入放在外部的 Python 和 TypeScript 示例里，测试时还能换成一个固定返回答案的 mock chooser。

另外两个 PR 在讨论怎样把这套流程延伸到视觉界面。

目前 jev-use 能运行的示例依然读取浏览器 DOM。规划中的 cua-perception 会作为可选的本地 Rust worker，把截图解析成文字、图标和对应区域，再交给应用代码构造候选动作。

Jev 自身仍然不用看图。图像解析由另一层完成，Jev 处理整理后的状态和候选项。不过，这部分还没有完整实现，当前 Draft 主要是在搭 worker 协议和截图记录等基础设施，没有接上生产推理模型。

RFC 里写得很细的一点，是每个候选动作必须对应到某一次具体截图。

比如你截了图，识别出一个按钮，但窗口随后移动、缩放，或者页面滚动了。原来的坐标看起来还是合法数字，点下去却可能已经是别的东西。

所以它计划把截图原始数据、目标窗口和坐标转换关系一起保存，让视觉识别结果与动作都绑定到这次观察。每次观察最多派生一次执行，操作之后重新读取状态，超时或者结果不明时也不能直接重放。

而且识别到一块像按钮的区域，只能算视觉观察，不能自动证明它可以点击。候选动作怎么构造、哪些动作允许执行，仍然由应用和 Driver 检查。

这比单独讨论模型多聪明更接近 computer use 的实际问题。模型选对了动作，也可能用错截图坐标；工具调用返回成功，也可能根本没改变应用状态。

当前表单示例会在提交后读取独立的 /state 接口，确认服务器确实收到了指定内容，不靠模型宣布完成。

当然，这个示例很小。代码每一步只提供下一个有效动作和 abstain，也就是放弃执行。当前提交通过的 CI 用的是 mock chooser，证明这套观察、选择、执行、验证的流程能够接通，还不能拿来证明 Jev 擅长复杂桌面任务。

真正难的部分会落到候选动作生成上。正确动作必须先出现在候选集合里，Jev 才有机会选中。如果每一步还得让大模型读完整个界面、想好全部参数，再交给 Jev 选一次，就需要算清楚整条流程到底省了多少时间。对于能用代码直接生成候选项的重复操作，这种分工才更容易发挥速度优势。

Jev VS Fable 5.1 VS GPT-6 Astra: chess

typesafe's new Jev V13 isn't an LLM. it doesn't chat, doesn't explain, doesn't write code — it only makes decisions. so we made it play blitz against frontier LLMs.

• astra didn't bother winning on material. it mated jev in 18 moves. Qe1#, with 2:27 to spare

t:
随便跑来源不明的 Agent Skill 和 MCP 配置，等同于在本地裸奔。如何在安装前，安全审查它们有没有偷走凭据？

开源新工具 jev-security-scan 提供了「零执行」的审查方案。它结合本地静态检查与 TypeSafe Jev，在不启动服务、不安装依赖的情况下，提前扫出代码里的隐蔽行为。

主要特性：
• 拒绝“下载即中招”：只读取目标文本、配置和脚本，完全不执行目标代码，从根本上防止触发恶意安装钩子。
• 精准抓取证据：若发现窃取 SSH 私钥、提示词注入或越权外传，会直接输出具体文件、行号与脱敏后的代码段。
• 极简无依赖：仅依赖 Python 3.10+ 标准库，连 pip install 都省了，天然支持作为 Codex 或 Claude Code 的 Skill 直接调用。
• 双模式切换：高敏感项目可使用 local 纯离线静态检查；常规项目开启 jev 模式进行深度语义分析。

对于经常折腾各种开源 Agent 扩展的开发者，在运行新框架前，用它过一遍“X光”是非常实用的防线。

t:
有点燃炸, 这才是 AI 自动化测试最狂暴的打开方式, 建议全屏静音把这几十秒百路并发狂测的演示看完, 去感受一下什么叫真正的工程降维打击。
前 Zapier AI Agent 负责人 Rafal Wilinski 刚晒出的这套对抗测试套件, 直接把整个 QA 圈看傻了。每次代码发布, 直接调动百路无头浏览器并发狂轰滥炸, 死命寻找能搞崩前端系统的边界缺陷, 跑完一整轮的成本竟然只有几美分。
很多团队以前尝试用大模型写端到端测试, 基本上全踩进了同一个坑: 鼠标点一下要等大模型在云端思考 3 到 5 秒, 跑完几十个用例烧掉几十刀不说, 还动不动遇到 JSON 格式崩溃或者把测试跑死在半路上。
真正让我觉得有意思的是, Rafal 根本没有用传统聊天模型, 他接入了专门输出强类型决策的 Jev。
最核心的质变是把文本生成降级为状态单选。以前的大模型在努力写小作文, 这里的模型只接收页面当前状态和一组预设动作, 在 100 毫秒内直接单选出破坏力最高的操作, 没有废话, 也不存在格式幻觉, 话音没落动作已经执行完毕。
这一步直接打通了成本的死穴。由于底层模型只对输入计费, 官方定价每百万 Token 仅 0.042 美元, 输出完全不花钱, 这意味着测试套件可以肆无忌惮地进行多路并发探索, 哪怕分出上百条执行链路去尝试畸形输入, 边际成本也几乎等于零。
更耐人寻味的是测试逻辑的倒置。以前写自动化脚本, 是人在已知用例里小心翼翼求证系统正常; 现在的对抗测试, 是放出一群不知疲倦的数字破坏狂, 在每个边界点上疯狂试探你的前端极限。
以前是人写死脚本去验证预期, 从今天起是 AI 扮演黑客在并发世界里暴力寻找意外。
这套打法不仅能测 Web 端, 几乎所有带状态机的交互都能被重写一遍。
如果把这种对抗测试挂进你们的发布流水线, 你最想让它去轰炸哪个页面? 我先说, 购物车结账和第三方授权回调, 以前人工测到吐的地方最该交给它。
完整的三层架构链路和接入逻辑, 我整理好沉在一楼了。 https://x.com/rafalwilinski/status/2100882207879434359/video/1

t:
This video is a concept, not the product.  

Get the first leads for free at https://redreplier.com and get early access to the JEV integration!

Jev makes a strong case for a dedicated decision layer in application design and marketing work.

a surprising amount of that work comes down to a small judgment:

→ which model should handle this request?
→ which topic or hook fits this post?
→ does this draft need human review?

here's how the pieces fit:

Jev: take the relevant context, answer bounded questions, return choices and probabilities.

code: apply rules and thresholds, enforce permissions, route the work.

LLM: write the response, draft the campaign, or handle deeper reasoning.

independent questions can run together. uncertain decisions can go to a stronger model or a person.

the part worth getting right is the handoff. a valid label can still be wrong. confidence needs checking against your own examples.

start with one low-risk decision. run it beside the current workflow. count the mistakes and review work alongside the model cost.

that's how a cheap model earns a place in the workflow.

q.t:
Jev classified 1,315 X posts for about $0.086 in estimated model cost 😂

seeing everyone's Jev demos made me want to build something for my own content research.

i'd collected a lot of posts, but figuring out what they had in common still meant opening them one by one and taking notes.

so i built a dashboard around Jev. it labels each post across 8 dimensions, including topic, hook and writing style.

now i can filter by topic and hook, compare engagement, and open the original posts to see the examples behind each pattern.

my archive is a lot easier to learn from now.

t:
I found Jev (@TypeSafe) very promising for computer use and browser agents, especially for lower latency and LLM cost on tasks that are purely about choosing from what's on screen.

Computer and browser use kept getting better with every new model, but it all rested on the model being smart enough to take a screenshot, reason about the image, and move forward, and every step burned more tokens. At this point, I eat through Astra credits in hours. Using LLMs for heavy and scalable CUA was too expensive.

Tool selection, target element, operation type, and state are all classifications over a closed set and should have been treated as one when handling them via agents, but so far I "let the LLM handle it" because it was easy.

q.t:
you can make any open source model behave like jev with just a bit of inference engineering.  

it's shockingly easy. to prove it, we built a new endpoint we're calling deepseek-v4.1-flash-jev. see the demo below. here's how it's done:

sglang (an inference engine) offers a scoring endpoint in addition to the normal generation one. in scoring mode, given an input & set of possible answers, it forces the model to produce probabilities for each one. example:

> input: what is most common letter in abcccde?
> possible answers: a, b, c
> output: (c, 0.9), (b, 0.0.5), (a, 0.05)

getting the above behavior instead of streamed output is as simple as using sglang's /v1/score endpoint instead of /generate. there's just one other trick required.

for deepseek, you have to add a closing think tag before the response. this forces a direct answer instead of  a reasoning trace. if you want reasoning, you can do that too, but imo that makes things too slow to be worth it.

dsv4.1 flash is not as good as jev, but if we had enough spare compute to experiment with this same approach for a larger model then i think the decision quality would be at least as good, if not better.

also, somewhat unrelated, i think decision-making models kill all prospecting & sourcing work. i would have absolutely killed to have jev or similar when i was recruiting @mintlify. absolutely incredible.

q.t:
I got access to Jev earlier today (thank you @hackgoofer).  I have run ~5,000 requests so far, (which cost me around $2!), across classification, model routing, intent, steering, and many other things.

tl;dr, Jev enables a new intelligent decision-making primitive, separate from deterministic code and LLM calls.  This allows a class of decision-making that was neither suited to dumb, unintelligent code, nor to slow, expensive LLMs.

It is super fast and cheap, and I think I will likely end up making a few Jev calls to every LLM call I make in my product. I think probably any company using LLM requests today can probably add a Jev call pre and/or post LLM calls to quite literally make their product much better for free, and have better tool calling behavior in many cases.  

I happened to have a personal benchmark for this as I’d been working on a ton of proactivity and classification tasks.  I have been using the deepseek flash and more recently gpt 5.6 luna family of models as reasonably smart classifiers with low latency.  Think questions like:

- Did this conversation output contradict something they’ve mentioned before?
- Should we send a followup message to this user based on our rules?
- It’s been a few seconds of silence.  Should we proactively send a message?

In the past, I’ve been forced to write a bunch of what I call decision chains, mostly because an LLM classification call is very expensive in TIME (avg 4s), and less importantly can cost quite a bit if run on every message.

Imagine a normal chat app.  If you added 4s to every response to figure out if the response is good before sending it out, that ends up being pretty bad.  So instead, I usually have to write some code that is a crude heuristic that runs quickly and decides whether to run the classifier.  Obviously this sucks because you call the classifier many times that you don’t want to, which makes your p95 bad, and you also miss cases with the heuristic, and you also have to manage all of these weird chains.

With Jev, it’s cheap enough, and fast enough (p50 ~150ms, p95 ~350ms in my testing!) that you can easily run it every turn.  Heck you can reasonably run it before generation AND post generation, for any application that isn’t realtime voice, and still feel snappy.

But this is just one use case.  Think: smarter model routing, better context packing, better responses, better observability for intent/tags/safety, smarter retries and so much more.  By simply thinking about the inputs and outcomes you want to enforce, you can use Jev to supercharge most model calls and reduce bad user outcomes.  The more “quirks” a model has, the more valuable it ends up being.

It’s a bit weird and unintuitive using Jev.  Generally, you want to decrease the # of questions you ask a classifier, or it makes more mistakes.  In fact, you might want to ask your questions kind of in a compound way, because the reasoning happens in a shared scratchpad of sorts.  Adding questions muddies the scratchpad and makes it take longer.  

With Jev, you feel incentivized to go the other way, to formulate your query as a set of independent questions.  It doesn’t feel like adding more questions decreases your performance on others.

You can go a bit deeper to improve tool calls.  Many model tools are things like turning on settings, or other things.  You can easily improve models that are not very good at tool calling with Jev, by simply figuring out when to run them.  You can do a pre-LLM call to figure out when to unfurl different tool definitions, in order to make your main LLM run better, you could run a background task with Jev + another LLM to reduce tool and context burden on your main LLM, and free it to be responsive.

I’ve only scratched the surface of my testing but very excited!

which sound effect?

tr: Jeth is different than ChatJPT or Claude in one big way. He can't write. It is a really good classifier. You describe your categories in plain English and it gives back responses in one or three ways. One, it can pick from the list you give it. Is this support ticket for billing or technical or sales? And it can respond back like consider technical 85% sure. Two, yes or no? They call it null, so a question like is the customer asking for refund? And Jeth's response could be 0.95, which means it's leaning heavily towards yes. Three, a score on a scale you write. Like how angry is the customer? Calm, frustrated or furious? Jeth could save 1.6 between frustrated and furious. Now because it can't write, it cannot invent answer, it cannot hallucinate. And it comes back in a fraction of a second at the fraction of the cost. So the bottom line is ChatJPT is built for your chatting or talking, whereas Jeth is built for your structured logical statements.

t:
A LOT changed in AI just yesterday and you NEED to know why.

** NOT CLICKBAIT**

A company called TypeSafe AI just came out of stealth. 

They're launching a new class of model that is built to sit between code and LLMs.

Today we two options: code (deterministic, cheap, doesn't hallucinate) and LLMs (flexible, expensive, occasionally hallucinates). 

This new model gives you a third option: fast, cheap, probability based outputs that your code can act on directly.

Here's an example: Say 1,000 leads come into your pipeline. Instead of burning LLM tokens scoring every single one, this kind of model can return something like "95% probability this is an enterprise lead" for a fraction of the cost.

The high confidence enterprise leads route to the sales team. The self serve leads get an automated demo email. You only spend real LLM budget on the leads that actually need deeper reasoning, like enrichment for your highest value prospects.

That's a huge shift in cost and speed.

I suspect this will be a pretty massive breakthrough that gets implemented fast into the software you are already using today.

tr: I'm Diego Almeida, founder of Typesafe AI, and at OpenAI, I co-created ChatGBT and RLHF, the post-training algorithm behind most frontier AI. Our team trained the first models to be superhuman at instruction following, what we now call Chat. And we asked ourselves, are models that are superhuman at Chat AGI? The answer was obviously not, but the trillion dollar question is why not? RLHF has led to LMs that are optimizing for human preferences and include issues such as mode dropping, overconfidence, and an overall lack of reliability. These flaws mean that LMs require humans in the loop, and almost no true automation can be done. At Typesafe, we've spent two years building in stealth, and we're finally ready to share our new type of foundation model that's optimized for automation. System 1 models. With a new architecture, new sampler, and new training algorithm, reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions. Movements are clear if you see them side by side. Ask a System 1 model a ton of structured questions, just like you would an LM. Get the answers back near instantly. Meanwhile, LMs take hundreds of times longer to finish responding. Look at how the LM generates sequentially, which is great for a natural conversation, but totally useless for computers. LMs extract intelligence from the tiny straw of auto regression, and similar to the jump that transformers made over RNMs, We are replacing sequential computation with parallel, because that is obviously the future. Our System 1 models output decisions with probabilities and confidence instead of words, and they can't hallucinate. They're a lot more like code, reliable, fast, self-consistent, and Typesafe. This opens up a whole new world of possibilities and applications. Today, we're releasing JIV, the first public System 1 model. It's 100 times faster, so real-time AI is finally possible. This is cheaper with input tokens priced at $42 per billion tokens, and output tokens are free because they're finally too f***ing cheap to meter. JIV is super smart, and its intelligence per dollar is literally off the charts. This is just the beginning. We're excited to see what you build with JIV. As we say at Typesafe, we're building prod, not God. We're waiting seconds for responses or paying for words you never asked for. Side effects may include fewer retries, fewer parsers, fewer broken schemas, and intelligence running inside every software loop. Your software may begin moderating every message, routing every ticket, reviewing every document, and making millions of background decisions that were previously too slow or expensive to automate. Entire software categories may be rewritten in the process. As costs fall, usage may increase dramatically. Ask your developer if your industry is ready.

t:
Jev @CompleteSkeptic dropped a few days ago, and the most interesting part isn’t the benchmark.

It’s what people are already building with it.
Browser agents. Code review. Skill routing. NPCs. Trading bots. Drone logic. Email triage.

The pattern is becoming pretty clear:
Jev is turning into an “AI if statement.”
A thread on the best community examples I’ve found ↓
 
⸻
 
1/ Browser agents
@browser_use built jev-ultrafast.
Their Flights demo reportedly finishes in ~7.1s.
Makes sense when you look at what a browser agent actually does all day:
click this or that?
continue or retry?
did the page satisfy the condition?
which action should happen next?
A lot of that doesn’t need full text generation.
It just needs a fast decision.
http://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast
 
⸻
 
2/ Jev as an MCP tool
@jkudish built jev-mcp.
It lets agents use Jev for things like:
claim verification
prompt injection checks
ranking
classification
This is probably one of the most obvious fits.
Instead of:
LLM → reasoning → JSON → parse → if
you can move toward:
Jev → probabilities → if
http://github.com/jkudish/jev-mcp
 
⸻
 
3/ Code review
@devagrawal09 built jev-review.
Instead of asking one model:
“review this entire PR”
the workflow breaks review into smaller decisions:
is there a likely bug?
did the API behavior change?
is there a security concern?
does this need human review?
That decomposition feels very native to this kind of model.
http://github.com/devagrawal09/jev-review
 
⸻
 
4/ Skill routing
GitHub user GodsBoy built jev-agent-skill-router.
The author reports 94.4% routing accuracy.
This one is especially interesting to me.
Once agents have 50, 100, or 500 skills, deciding which skill to call becomes its own model problem.
Do we really want a giant LLM rereading every tool description on every turn?
Probably not.
http://github.com/GodsBoy/jev-agent-skill-router
 
⸻
 
5/ NPC behavior
@haiderTheDev built Hollow Creek.
Instead of using a large model for every NPC action, Jev can sit in the loop and answer smaller questions:
scared?
approach?
run?
attack?
trust the player?
That feels much closer to a game “reflex system” than a chatbot.
http://hollow-creek-sigma.vercel.app
 
⸻
 
6/ Trading every block
@jarrodwatts built jev-trader.
Every block, Jev decides:
BUY / SELL / HOLD
No idea if it makes money 😅
But the interesting part is the frequency.
There are lots of places where nobody would previously call an LLM because the decision is too small, too frequent, or too latency-sensitive.
That changes if inference becomes cheap enough.
http://github.com/jarrodwatts/jev-trader
 
⸻
 
7/ Drone decision layer
GitHub user RomanSlack built jev-drone.
The interesting architecture isn’t “AI controls the whole drone.”
It’s more like:
large model = planning fast decision model = tactical reflexes
That separation may end up being important far beyond drones.
http://github.com/RomanSlack/jev-drone
 
⸻
 
8/ One score per pixel
GitHub user rivianpratama built JevPixelArt.
Each pixel effectively becomes a scoring decision.
This is exactly the kind of thing that sounds absurd with a normal LLM.
But once inference is cheap enough, suddenly people start putting models inside loops that used to be completely deterministic.
Demo: http://jevpixel.vercel.app
Repo: http://github.com/rivianpratama/JevPixelArt
 
⸻
 
9/ The boring business use cases may matter more
Near Here tested Jev for local event validation.
They reported 96% on 50 examples.
ActionBox explored refund review with human escalation.
@DisruptConcept used it for desktop email triage.
There’s also an anonymous legal-tech test on 9,840 Enron emails.
None of these are flashy.
But classification, filtering, routing, moderation, prioritization and review are basically everywhere inside real software.
A huge amount of business logic is just:
fuzzy if statements.
thanks @santiagocasti, it's been a pleasure working with you during early access

q.t:
Chat told me to build open source jev for the next YT project

That would be fun. I am thinking of using a bidirectional attention transformer and borrow ideas from masked LM training.

Training data + prompt format + loss fn are the main unknowns. I will generate synthetic datasets in the 
<PROMPT> <CHOICES> <JSON OUTPUT> format, and train only on the json values instead of the full JSON string (i.e. the schema is fixed & guaranteed to follow the structured out).

In other words, a fill-in-the-blank model with verifiable outputs. So one can even do RLVR training.

I am not sure what the best architecture for the output-head is - these all seem doable: 

(a) Train it over a list of special tokens such as "CHOICE_1", "CHOICE_2" etc. The choices get passed int he prompt, and we train using standard cross-entropy loss.

OR, (b) it could do some kind of encoder-decoder architecture where it matches the embedding of the actual choices against the masked token embedding. Like a contrastive loss

OR, (c) it actually generates probabilities over the entire vocab and uses constrained decoding to figure out the best choice from the available list of choices. This technically requires an autoregressive LM to generate the tokens using llguidance/outlines stuff - so I am pretty sure that this is not what JEV does

Lets see, currently leaning towards (b)

Since folks have asked, I think the future is likely:

- a mixture of deterministic code and agentic execution. today, tons of tokens in “loops” are wasted. you do not need to run an agent every 5 mins to find PRs that just hit prod - code is cheaper, faster, and more reliable 
- a mixture of long lived code (that can be continuously evaluated and improved), and one-off scripts for dynamic execution 

This is similar to Claude Code dynamic workflows (which are still very slept on), except optimized for always-on durable execution in the cloud (temporal style).

t:
BTW, this is *made* for dspy.Flex.

Because Flex exposes the Module's code and instructions to optimizers, it will often decompose a program into multiple modules. A deep research task might get split into Search and Write, for example.

With Jev, we want to decompose *output fields*, not modules. Say you're triaging an email to determine if it requires a reply. Your DSPy signature might have one output field, a bool for 'should_reply'.

A Jev/Flex approach to optimizing that optimizing that program might break it down into sub questions, which we could render as modules or output fields, which we later roll up. Like: `not_spam`, `asks_for_reply`, `timely`, etc.

The price & speed here are the difference between something that ~works~ as a consumer app vs. something that’s completely infeasible.

Excited to see the apps that Jev unlocks.

Also I’m kind of surprised it didn’t need a deeper reasoning model for this! But I’ll take it 😅

Testing two things in OpenChamber 1.24.1. Both off by default.

→ Auto model routing: pick "Auto" and each prompt gets its own model, thinking level and agent — cheap and fast for a quick question, strong for a big refactor. Rules are editable in Settings.

10分で作ったやつ、Opusと5時間いじってこうなりました。

trueX（トゥルー・エックス）は、X（Twitter）タイムライン上の投稿をリアルタイムで解析し、「公式発表」「未確認の噂」「個人の感想」「ネタ・デマ注意」をスマートに色分け表示するChrome拡張機能です。

文章を生成しない次世代AI「TypeSafe AI (Jev)」の超高速判定（200ms台）により、ブラウジングを妨げることなく、タイムラインの情報信頼度を一目で把握できます。

【主な機能】
⚡ 超高速リアルタイム判定
タイムラインを流し見しながら、各投稿の事実裏付け確率や確信度スコアを200ms台で瞬時に判定・表示します。

🎯 スマートな4層コンテキスト分類
・📢 公式発表・事実（青）：確定した一次情報や公式ニュースをハイライト
・🟡 未確認の噂・リーク（黄）：未確認情報を「デマ」と決めつけず、注意喚起で表示
・💭 個人のつぶやき・感想（グレー）：日常のつぶやきを邪魔せず、静かに共存
・🔴 虚偽・デマ・ネタ注意（赤）：明らかなホラ話やフェイク情報を確率付きで看破

🎛️ ラベル別の表示カスタマイズ
ポップアップからラベルごとに表示・折りたたみを自由に切り替え可能。「個人の感想は折りたたんで、速報や噂だけをチェックする」といった快適なタイムライン閲覧が可能です。

---

触ってみた開発メモ：
・ラベルごとに折りたたみの選択ができる（ただ折りたたみUIがいまいちなので直すのが課題）
・以前Gemini 2.5 Flash-Liteで同様のを作ってたけど、TypeSafeの判定が別次元に速い（200ms台）
・今日開発で1,600判定くらいしてるけど$0.05。最初にチャージされた$5が、まだ$4.95残ってる

あとは今日中にCWS（Chrome Web Store）に申請。といってもサイト作って、ストア原稿作って、申請後にnote書いて、X告知で終了って感じ。

q.t:
Okay so Jev can actually do computer use really well

Without any screenshots, or LLMs and no Pixels leave my mac 

I dont even read the Dom elements

A local CoreML model segments every button and UI element on screen. 

On-device OCR reads the labels. That text is all Jev gets.

It returns a probability across those elements and tells me the best one to click.

Then it clicks, re-runs detection, and decides again. In a loop until the goal is done.

~90ms per decision. Faster than any LLM computer use I've tried.

Blazing fast computer use, without any latency

@typesafeai is building something really interesting

文章を書かないAIで、業務の自動化はどこまで変わるのか。TypeSafe AIが発表したJevは、決められた選択肢と確率を返すことに特化したモデルです。速さや安さも目を引きますが、注目したいのは、AIの判断を普通のソフトウェアに組み込む設計。その仕組みと、数字を見るときの注意点を整理しました。

【文章を捨てて、判断に特化。Jevは何が違う？】

🧩 「コード＋AI」で自動化を組み立てる新モデル

■ 1. 会話より、分類・振り分け
  ▸ Jevは自由な文章を生成せず、あらかじめ定義した構造・選択肢に沿って判断を返す。問い合わせの分類、担当への振り分け、採点などが想定用途。
  ▸ 各出力に確率・確信度が付き、周囲のコードが次の処理を決める。現在は早期アクセスで、待機リストから順次案内。

■ 2. 速さの鍵は並列出力
  ▸ 文章をトークンごとに順番に生成する代わりに、複数の判断を並列に出力。RLCDという学習法で、確率と実際の正答率が対応する判断を目指す。
  ▸ 同社公表は応答70〜500ms、入力100万トークン$0.042、出力無料。自社ワークフロー評価では193.6倍高速・444.6倍安価と報告。

■ 3. 「型エラーなし」と「誤判断なし」は別
  ▸ 保証の対象は出力が定義した型に合うこと。請求の問い合わせを技術に分類するような、意味上の間違いまで消えるわけではない。
  ▸ 評価の参照はGPT-6 AstraとFable 5.1の平均で、正解ラベルではない。倍率も実業務の改善幅の上限寄り、と同社は説明。
  ▸ 導入するなら小さな分類業務から。誤判断率を測り、曖昧なケースを人へ戻す条件と、実行ルールを決めて使う。

🔗 TypeSafe AI｜System One Models & Jev
https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev

q.t:
TypeSafe「Jev」、面白そう👀
タスクを細かく分解して、ここを判定し判断軸を持たせるということのよう。

元OpenAIのDiogo Almeidaらが
「チャットではすでに超人がいるのに、なぜ仕事は自動化されないのか」と問い、2年かけて出した判断専用モデル。

・入力は問い合わせ文やアプリの状態。
・返すのは「どの部署か」「緊急か」「基準を満たすか」といった型付きの答えと、その確率と信頼度。

文章は書かない。
その代わり速く、安く、プログラムがそのまま読める。

チャットの進化形ではなく「コードの中で使える賢いif文」。
それが正体。

既存LLMとの差は、強さの種類にある。

「LLMは人向け」
返信の下書き、要約、対話、長い推論は強い。
だが遅くて高く、JSONが壊れたり、自信過剰になったりする。
人が読んで直す前提が残る。

「Jevは機械向け」
出力の形を先に固定し、校正された確率だけを出す。
壊れた文字列で処理が止まらない。
自信が低ければ、そこで自動実行を止められる。

知能を増やす話というより、ソフトウェアが信頼して分岐できる形にした話のようだ。

LLMとの使い分けは置き換えではない。
・決まった計算や権限はコード
・意味の判定を何度も回すならJev
・文章を生む工程だけLLM

たとえばサポートなら、
・返品期限の判定はコード
・緊急度と担当部署と返金可否はJev
・お客様への返信文はLLM

エージェントなら、
・LLMが調べて書き、
・Jevが「正しい文脈を拾ったか」「出力は基準を満たすか」を途中で検査する

大きな問いを一発で投げず、狭い質問に分解してコードで合成する。
そこが本番に載るかの分かれ目になる。

これから変わるのは、画面のチャットより裏側だ。
判断が安く何度も呼べると、生成のたびに検査し、怪しいときだけ高いモデルや人に渡せる。

自動化は「一発で賢い答えを出す」ことから、「安く検証しながら進む」ことへ寄っていく。

競争も、何でも話せるかより、コードに埋め込んで止まらず動くかへ移る。

これは「神を作り出す」という話ではなく「現場の分岐を信頼できる部品にする」というストーリー。

q.t:
"DiffusionGemma as Jev" showcases the power of non-autoregressive architectures.

While Jev demonstrates the value of rapid decision models, running DiffusionGemma in this paradigm leverages canvas diffusion to evaluate structured choices in a single parallel pass:

⚡ ️Massive Parallelism: Denoises across an open canvas in a single step instead of sequential autoregressive token generation (~0.2s on a DGX spark).

🧠 Full Bidirectional Attention: Allows every option to attend to the full context concurrently, yielding well-calibrated decision distributions.

👁️ Multimodal Grounding: Inherits Gemma 4's spatial vision capabilities for complex visual and text decisions.

Read more about this approach here:
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57250

t:
Update: as some folks have commented it appears to be “calibrated” with a version of Platt’s scaler aka temperature scaling. 

If true it is a rather dumb idea considering that:

1) Platt’s scaler was invented specifically for support vector machines assuming specific shape of class scores. 

2) relies on very restrictive assumptions which have been proven basically assumes normality and homoscedasticity of class scores. 

3) can make miscalibration worse

TL;DR when one reads scikit learn fairytales about calibration things are bound to happen.

q.t:
@fakegingerbitch asked and I checked.

Here is what I quickly found:

TypeSafe sells its AI model Jev on one promise: when it says "70% likely", it's right about 70% of the time.

I tested that on 8 real datasets — loan defaults, bankruptcies, medical diagnoses, marketing responses. 16,500 predictions.

It fails on 7 of 8.

Jev is 10× more miscalibrated than CatBoost, a standard model anyone can download for free. On average it's no more useful than guessing the overall rate for every single case.

And it fails in one direction: it thinks bad things are about twice as likely as they really are. Loan defaults, bankruptcies, disease — all overstated, on every dataset.

German loan data: applicants flagged "critical account" repay 83% of the time. Jev says 26%.

The fix takes 120 rows of data and a textbook method from 2017. 

It removes three quarters of the error. A model that was actually calibrated would gain nothing from that.

Calibration is something you measure. Not something you announce.

* Decide — same weights, one forward pass, new head, no decode.  For fast parallel decision making (jev-like)

知道了 Jev 能用在哪

这条直接帮你梳理这些场景适不适合你，
以及能不能自己跑通闭环：

1. 操作电脑  
适合已经在用 Codex / Claude Code，但嫌 computer use 又慢又卡的人。  

简单动作可以闭环：Jev 判断点哪里，Agent 直接执行；复杂界面仍建议留人工接管。

2. 操作浏览器  
适合要自动搜、比价、填表、做网页流程的运营和开发。  

目标窄、按钮有限时能闭环；
页面一乱、要自己理解新站点，就还得大模型补位。

3. 海量分流和分类  
适合客服、运营、公关这种每天要处理大量进件的人。  

高置信度可以全自动分部门、打标签；
拿不准的再转人工，这是最容易先跑通的闭环。

4. 模型路由  
适合自己做 AI 产品、背后挂了好几个模型的人。
  
闭环很完整：用户一句话进来，Jev 选模型，生成接口直接出活。

5. 内容批量分析  
适合创作者、增长，想搞清楚「什么内容真的涨」。 
 
单次分析不是闭环，只是出结论；把结果接回「写稿 → 打分 → 再写」才算闭环。

6. 信息流过滤  
适合时间线被广告、引战、回复侠刷屏的人。 
 
可以闭环：帖子出现 → Jev 判断 → 隐藏或留下，人不用再看第二眼。

7. 代码审查和安全门禁  
适合带团队的开发，以及会自动改代码、跑命令的 Agent

不建议全自动闭环。高置信度拦截可以自己完成，放行和合并还是留给人或大模型。

8. 交易决策  
适合在做策略、回测、交易机器人的人。  

演示里可以闭环：价格进来，买或卖出去。真金白银不要全交给它，低置信度和风控必须留人手。

9. 游戏和实时控制  
适合做游戏 AI、实时控制和高频 Agent 的人。
  
天生就是闭环：状态进来，100 毫秒给出动作，环境更新后再判断下一拍。

Jev 负责判断，
闭环成不成，看你有没有把「判断之后的那一下」接好~

t:
Trusted monitoring is the backbone of AI Control. LLMs as a monitor have been fairly accurate, but are quite expensive and inconsistent.

When @typesafeai released Jev, I spent $1.09 dollars and ~15 hours analyzing it - a non-generative model as a monitor alternative for AI Control. Its only goal is to answer a yes/no question with a probability.

My pilot findings show that:
> it's a real first-pass monitor  - 90% of backdoors caught at 2% audit budget (FPR)
> but it can be selected against - lets the attacker test 4 variants and catch rate drops to 67%

Full write-up: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/d7pQicW8EhpPBDRqz/a-non-generative-model-as-a-trusted-monitor-for-ai-control

q.t:
jev 本质是专门服务于结构体生成的高速模型，在已经非常宽泛的 LLM 需求里，专门挑了一个刚需单独做

而结构体确实是 AI 工作的水电煤

2023 年的时候，开发者会先完成 tool 内的代码，然后使用 few shots 让 AI 生成对应的 json 结构体，再把结构体送入专门的执行器

用这个思路，可以完成 tool 调用、分类器、决策器等一系列功能，langchain 有一个标准 chain 就是用来做 routing 的

甚至在更早的 GPT-3 时期，AI 甚至没有 tool calls 的 schema 约束能力，开发者已经在采用 few shots 的方式去做结构体的输出和消费，可以说在语言模型发展的早期，结构体就是最早的 AI 工作流水电煤

到了 2025 年，AI 生成代码的能力开始显著变强，以 claude code 为首的 coding harness 倾向于使用 bash 和临场编写代码的方法完成复杂任务，与此同时随着一系列 skills 和 cli 的普及，“结构体”似乎变成了被 AGI 进程吞噬的一个小小概念

但结构体的生产和消费确实太高频了，CLI 调用本质是结构体，tool calls 本质是结构体，时常也大量存在用 2B 小模型做路由的需求、这个也是结构体

因此，在 2026 年，专注于结构体这一个需求的模型，再次火起来也是有合理性的

一个简单的功能是按需路由，把 prompt提前分配给不同尺寸的模型进行工作，尽管具体实现上还有缓存之类的问题，但不可否认的是，这个需求确实就是“语义进去，结构体出来，最好又快又便宜”

我一直有个观点是，AI 是未来生活的水电煤，结构体又是 AI 工作的水电煤

Examples:

I’m particularly excited about the future of computer use and Jev, seemingly as it’s extremely fast (and hella cheap)

API cost / wall time / outcome:

Jev finished at ~1/315 of GPT-6’s API cost and ~26% of its wall time, including API waits. 

Mini hit the cycle limit.

Note: ~88% of wall time was spent waiting for API responses. This only reflects current implementation—not Jev’s maximum control rate.

I think the new Jev model by @typesafeai is a very big deal. I think of it as :

LLMs are made for chat, and we have workarounds to use them for software logic and workflows.  Basically we ask this general-purpose model to write JSON for us. All that can be malformed, and it often is. It often isn't consistent, so we have a lot of workarounds for that.  And we need to use more expensive and slower models than feels like should be necessary, and all that adds cost and latency.

Jev has the general-purpose intelligence like LLMs, but is scoped down to classification tasks. What that means is it can be a very, very fast general-purpose classifier. There are a ton of use cases where training and fine-tuning a classifier was worth it. There's a whole bunch where training a classifier would be very useful, but creating the dataset and then evaluating it and all that was just much higher lift than was worth it for an experiment. With Jev, you just do that everywhere. You don't have to fine-tune a model, and it's still pretty fast.

I think this is a huge deal because most software is a series of if statements or switch statements where we're trying to decide which path to go down.

So much so that people have been able to use Jev to drive browsers, play video games, write text via heavy classification and to do all sorts of things. Those are demos today, and TBD on how it all shakes out for which use cases.   But the point is that having a strong classifier that you don't have to fine-tune can do A LOT.

ar.ti: Jevとは？よくある質問FAQ形式でまとめてみた。
ar.tx:
OpenAIでRLHF（ChatGPTの基盤技術）を共同開発したDiogo Almeida氏）が、自らCEOを務めるTypeSafe AIから新しいAIモデル「Jev」を発表した。
主張の核心は「チャットで超人間的な性能を持つモデルが何年も前からあるのに、なぜAGIや大規模な自動化につながらないのか？」という問いです。
その答えとして、テキスト生成ではなく「ソフトウェアが直接使える構造化された判断」に特化した新しいクラスのモデルを作った、というのが発表の趣旨です。
2年間のステルス開発の成果として、2026年9月15日に公開されました。
 
1. そもそも何？
Q. Jevって何ですか？
A. 文章を書くAIではなく、「判断するAI」です。会話や作文ではなく、「どれを選ぶか」「何点か」「本当かどうか」を、決まった形で速く返します。
Q. ChatGPTと同じものですか？
A. 仲間ではありますが、用途が違います。ChatGPTは人と話す・文章を作るためのAI。Jevはソフトの中で判断を出すためのAIです。
Q. なぜ文章を書けないのですか？
A. 文章生成をやめることで、速く安く、形の崩れた答えが出にくくなるからです。卵を自由に調理するのではなく、最初から卵ケースに入れる機械、という考え方です。
Q. 名前の由来は？
A. 経済の「ジェボンズのパラドックス」からです。「効率が上がると、かえってたくさん使われる」という意味が込められています。知能が安くなると、今までAIを使えなかった場所でも使われるようになる、という狙いです。
Q. System Oneって何ですか？
A. 「速い直感的な判断」を指す呼び方です。人間が数秒で決めるような判断を、ソフトがそのまま使える形で出すモデル、という意味です。
2. 何ができて、何ができない？
Q. 会話できますか？
A. 基本的にできません。チャット相手ではありません。
Q. メールやレポートは書いてくれますか？
A. 書きません。書くのは普通の文章生成AIの仕事です。
Q. じゃあ何ができるのですか？
A. 例えば次のような判断です。
この問い合わせは「請求」「技術」「解約」のどれか
このお客さんは怒っているか
この内容はルール違反か
候補がたくさんあるとき、どれが一番よさそうか
Q. 普通の人が「これやって」とお願いできるのですか？
A. 今のところ、どちらかというとアプリや社内システムの中に組み込むものです。一般の人が単体アプリとして気軽に使う段階ではまだありません。
Q. 賢いのですか？ バカなのですか？
A. 「文章を書く賢さ」ではなく、「決まった問いへの判断の賢さ」を狙っています。作文は苦手、仕分けや採点は得意、という autobots です。
Q. 計算や難しい推理は得意ですか？
A. 長考が必要な問題を一発で解くモデルではありません。大きな問題は小さく分けて、ソフト側で組み合わせる使い方が想定されています。
3. 自分の生活や仕事に関係ある？
Q. 一般人でも使う機会はありますか？
A. 直接使うより、裏側で使われる可能性のほうが高いです。問い合わせ振り分け、審査、推薦、監視、ゲーム、検索の裏側などです。
Q. 仕事は奪われますか？
A. 「全部の仕事」より、「毎日同じ判断を繰り返す作業」が減る可能性はあります。最終判断や対人対応は残ることが多いです。
Q. ChatGPTは不要になりますか？
A. なりません。話す・書くAIと、判断するAIは役割が違います。両方使う世界のほうが自然です。
Q. 会社の人だけが得する話ですか？
A. 今は開発者・企業向けの発表です。一般の人が得を感じるのは、対応が速くなる、審査が早くなる、料金が下がる、といった間接的な形になりやすいです。
4. 速さ・安さ・正確さ
Q. 本当にそんなに速いのですか？
A. 発表側の主張では、同じ種類の判断なら通常の最先端AIより何十倍〜200倍速い、としています。体感では「チャットを待つ」ではなく「ボタンを押したらすぐ結果が出る」イメージです。
Q. 安いのですか？
A. 発表では、入力はかなり安く、出力は無料とされています。ただし実際の請求は使い方次第です。大量に回す会社ほど差が出やすいです。
Q. 嘘はつかないのですか？
A. 「変な文章を作る」意味での嘘は出にくいです。ただし判断そのものが間違うことはあります。自信の低さは数値で出る設計です。
Q. 100点の正解を出すのですか？
A. 違います。「たぶんこう」を確率つきで出すAIです。自信が高いときだけ自動で進め、低いときは人に回す、という使い方が想定されています。
Q. 会社の宣伝が盛っていませんか？
A. その疑問は健全です。今は主に自社発表とデモ中心で、第三者の長い実戦検証はまだこれからです。
5. 使い方のイメージ
Q. どうやって使うのですか？
A. 裏でプログラムが「今の状況」と「聞きたいこと」を送り、Jevが決まった形の答えを返します。人がチャット画面で話す、というより機械同士のやり取りです。
Q. 質問は日本語でいいのですか？
A. 自然言語の質問は理解する設計です。ただし今の公開情報だけでは、日本語の強さの詳細はまだわかりにくいです。
Q. 答えはどんな形で返ってきますか？
A. 「選択肢A、確率70%、自信は高め」のような、プログラムがすぐ使える形です。長い説明文ではありません。
Q. 確率で返ってきたら、結局人が決めるのでは？
A. その通りの場面もあります。違いは、全部を人が見なくてよくなることです。自信が高い案件だけ自動処理、怪しい案件だけ人が見る、という分け方ができます。
Q. 間違えたら誰の責任ですか？
A. AIが出した判断でも、運用する会社やサービスの責任になるのが普通です。だから「全部自動」より「自信の低いものだけ人に回す」使い方が現実的です。
6. お金、安全、今すぐ使えるか
Q. 無料ですか？
A. 一般向けの無料アプリというより、開発者・企業向けの有料サービスです。今はウェイトリスト（順番待ち）です。
Q. 個人で申し込めますか？
A. サイトから待てますが、優先されるのは実際にシステムへ組み込みたい開発者や企業が多いと思われます。
Q. 自分の文章や社内データを送っても大丈夫ですか？
A. 会社に確認が必要です。新しいサービスなので、データの保存期間、学習利用の有無、国外送信の有無を見るべきです。
Q. 秘密の情報が学習に使われますか？
A. 公開情報だけでは断定できません。使う前に利用規約とセキュリティ説明を確認するのが安全です。
Q. 今すぐ触れるデモはありますか？
A. 発表時にはデモ動画や一部プレイグラウンドの案内がありますが、誰でも無制限に使える状態ではありません。
7. 将来と本音の疑問
Q. これでAGI（人間並みの汎用AI）に近づくのですか？
A. 発表者は「自動化と経済インパクトへの近道」と見ています。ただしJev単体は万能脳ではなく、判断専用パーツです。
Q. 文章を書くAIと合体したら最強ですか？
A. その使い方が一番現実的です。書くAIが下書

t: Jev just proved that you don't need an LLM for every task
Jevの内部構造の推測

q.t:
Jevの内部アーキテクチャを推測している技術記事(Jev’s Architecture Unmasked)からメモ。

・本記事はJevのAPIを約1万回の呼び出して、内部構造を推測したもの

・従来の言語モデルを用いた分類やルーティングでは、トークンを1文字ずつ逐次生成するために膨大な無駄な計算コストが発生していた。
・JevはLLMの膨大な知識をそのまま保持しつつ、テキスト生成を完全に排除して内部表現から直接確率を出力する

・システム全体の構造は、共通の文脈をエンコードする共有状態、並列に処理される質問群、そして確率を直接読み出すヘッドの3要素から成立
・モデルは入力を左から右へ読む事前学習済みの因果トランスフォーマーであり、プロンプト処理の直後に推論を終了する
・テキスト生成ループは存在しない
・だから、単語の綴りやJSONのフォーマットを出力するためのステップが一切不要

・APIレスポンスに含まれる出力トークン数という項目は、単に返却された文字列の長さから、後で計算された課金用の指標にすぎない
・選択肢が2個の場合でも200個の場合でもサーバーの処理時間はほぼ変化せず、モデルがトークンを逐次生成していない事実を強く裏付けている

・入力データは共有状態と複数の質問に分割され、問い合わせ本文などの共通コンテキストは一度だけKVキャッシュに保存される
・複数の質問は同じ共有キャッシュを参照するため、質問数が増加しても共有状態を何度も再計算する必要がない

・それぞれの質問はお互いの存在や指示が見えないようになっている
・質問同士が干渉することなく完全に隔離された状態で推論される
・ある質問内に秘密のコードを記述しても別の質問からは参照できない
・共有状態に置いた場合のみ全質問から認識可能
・約100個の質問まではリクエストの処理時間がほとんど増加せず、共通状態を一度だけ計算して並列処理する設計の恩恵が明確に現れている

・Jevが持つ高度な知識水準を考慮すると、双方向エンコーダを新規開発したのではなく、既存の因果デコーダ型LLMを再利用した可能性が極めて高い

・トークナイザの挙動は既存の公開モデルと完全には一致しない
・数字の分割方法やチャンク処理に独自の工夫が見られる

・選択肢の並び順に関する実験では、判断の根拠となる情報が選択肢リストの末尾に配置されていてもモデルは正しく正解を選択できた
・質問に含まれる各選択肢は独立して採点されるのではなく、リスト全体が互いに文脈として影響を及ぼし合った上で判断される
・無関係なダミーの選択肢を追加すると既存の選択肢間の相対的なオッズ比が変化した
・このことから、選択肢同士が相互作用していることが実験的にわかる
・リスト全体を一括して読み込む設計のおかげで、上記のどれでもないといった他の選択肢に依存する回答も適切に処理できる
・選択肢の提示順序を逆転させると出力確率に若干の変動が生じるため、実務で特定の閾値を用いて自動処理を行う際は順序バイアスへの配慮が求められる

・学習手法にはRLCDと呼ばれる独自のアプローチが採用されている
・強化学習の枠組みを用いて真の結果に即した予測確率を出力するように調整されている

・モデルの出力は対数損失やブライア損失といった適格スコアリングルールで最適化され、正直な不確実性を反映した確率分布を形成する
・ベンチマークの検証結果において予測確率と実際の正解率は高精度に一致しており、期待キャリブレーション誤差は0.0313という極めて低い値を記録した

・難易度の高い数学問題ではモデルが提示する正解確率自体が低下する
・なので、自身の知識の限界に応じた不確実性を表現できている
・APIが返す信頼度スコアは学習された固有値ではなく、得られた確率分布の最大値から算術計算で求めた便宜的な数値にすぎない

・Jevのバックボーンには、必要な専門モジュールのみを選択的に起動するスパースなMixture of Expertsが採用されていると推測される
・テキスト生成を行わないプロンプト処理のみのタスクでは計算負荷がボトルネックとなるため、疎な構造による演算量削減が大きな効果を発揮する
・約3万トークンの入力をわずか160ミリ秒程度で処理する速度性能は、巨大な密結合モデルではなくMoEを採用している推測ともあう
・質問枝はチャットのような逐次的会話ではなく独立したバッチとして処理されるため、GPUリソースを最大限に活用した一括計算が可能

q.t:
some underrated points + important second order effects of the wildly successful Jev launch

1. Data is the bottleneck! TypeSafe calls themselves a “data research lab”. 

To build a general purpose classifier or actor of any kind, you need to painstakingly curate and create tons of high-quality data (Traces, Examples, Evals/Environments/Worlds, Simulations). 
This helps the model learn these distributions so it can do good work for users. This is especially true for building domain specific, vertical agents.

Look at the data. Every team looking to build better agents will need help + tooling to help them with this. If teams can spend more time building good data, then they will build better models & agents.

2. The explosion of ultra-cheap, always-on Monitoring + Data Mining of Agent Traces at scale

To build better agents, we need to understand them at scale. We also saw the large need to real-time monitor and flag bad behavior during the OpenAI-HuggingFace Incident. Models like Jev help us do this because they’re very fast and cheap for classification.

There’s a simple pipeline here:
Gather Traces —> Label Them aggressively —> Make Evals/Environments from them (optional) -> Fine-Tune Cheaper Model.

Part of data hygiene is understanding data at scale. We sort of had the tooling to do this before by fine-tuning small models or sending smart agents to read lots of traces. 
We’ll still use agents to mine traces because Jev has limitations like context window length, but this is a great tool for:
- humans to define dimensions up front on what they care
- using Jev to triage data across important dimensions for further review.

3. We are never escaping Jevon’s paradox

Models like Jev just help us do more. Classify more traces, monitor more actions in real-time. This is all net-new addition of compute and will happen at massive-scale over every piece of data agents create. 

This is all very exciting because though we’ll use more compute, we’ll understand much more to build better systems.

q.t:
you can just ask a model a question that requires a given output, from a list of up to 50,000 outputs, and then naively parse the next token it generates to do the same thing...?

"200x faster" okay yeah you're generating one token  and running a deterministic system with the output, good job?

am I completely misunderstanding this thing? seems not super impresssive. 

I do like the basically parallel instead of sequential inference idea, but you can do that with LLMs to by just putting the parallel processing you need in the prompt rather than having the model think through it. 

The whole "tiny straw of autoregression" thing is completely ignoring that you can just load yourself up 100 different KV caches and inference them all at once for one token. You don't have to use LLMs like a chatbot!?! 

this is among the reasons why we need to keep completions apis, and we just need better tooling for them....

this is one of my favorite under-used ways to inference LLMs, and it's exactly how the original DATA Browse would narrow down from 1000 potential sources to the 20 pages we actual read and parsed fully to conserve tokens, but it is *not* ...like.... new?

GPT-3 did this really well. all groq models do this brilliantly. 

you can get type safety and the rest off it by just inferencing in parallel in json mode with an affordable model. one token output 200 times is in fact nearly free, but it seems like with Jev and with other models you pay out the ass for context. such is life.

I will give several things to them though: incredible pink coat, and based as hell to name your product after a paradox.

TypeSafe AIが開発したJevが話題になっています。
Jevは文章の意味を読み取りソフトウェアが使える分類やスコアを返すこれまでのLLMとは処理の仕方が異なるAIモデルです。
判断を速く安く繰り返すという特性は、大量の文章を分析用データへ変換する工程と相性がよさそうです。

実際に公式も大量データの処理や予測に使う特徴量の抽出を用途として挙げています。
海外の開発者からもデータの分類や名寄せへの活用案が出ています。
データ基盤との接点は公式の提案と開発者の関心の両方に見られます。

今回はJevとは何か、どんな利点があるのかを整理し
既存のデータ基盤に組み込んだ場合の構成や現時点での海外の評価を洗ってみました。

■ 新しいAIモデルJevとデータ処理との親和性

Jevは文章などの入力を読み取り、あらかじめ定義した分類やスコアなどの判断を返すAIモデルです。
元OpenAI研究者らが設立したTypeSafe AIがソフトウェアに組み込む判断を自動化するために開発しました。

特徴は、あらかじめ決めた選択肢や形式に沿って結果を返す構造化出力に特化していることです。
例えば商品説明からカテゴリを選びその値を後続の処理へ直接渡せます。
LLMにも出力形式を制約する機能はありますが、Jevは文章生成を省いて複数の判断を並列に行う設計で速さと安さを追求しています。

同社の評価では比較対象のLLMよりおよそ200倍速く、費用は約400分の1としています。
これは改善幅が大きい側の結果で用途によって差は変わります。
それでも必要な精度が得られるなら大量のデータを1件ずつ分類する処理では魅力的です。

Jev can be extremely useful for economic research: of course classification tasks, but also with "simulated" surveys.

To illustrate, I ask 56,949 simulated NYCers a question, one for every adult in the Census Bureau's 2024 microdata sample of the city for less than 2 dollars.

of course we had to run jev on ori eval vs 4 other popular llm-as-a-judge/classification models 

jev came in at 5x faster than the next fastest, matched in accuracy with the next top model, and was 2nd cheapest at a 30-decision task 

not bad at all @typesafeai

q.t:
1/ Jev, a decision model by @typesafeai, sparked a burst of projects and discussion. We tested it using Ori Eval against popular LLMs on OpenRouter at judging.

Jev was >5x faster than the next fastest model, and even its slowest requests beat every other model's median.

t: so what I'm seeing so far is that jev like approaches work with pretrained llms but it's not really generalizing to abilities that they haven't been trained on. probably just a little more time until frontier labs bolt on classification head to claude or astra
If you're rushing to replace your LLM integrations with Jev, ask yourself whether you've done the evals to confirm it's delivering the quality you want, not just cost and speed benefits.
What if Jev was a tool that LLMs could call to get confidence in an action?

Indeed. Jev has kickstarted an explosive growth cycle in discriminative models in open source, that will start to form the backbone of more and more harnesses. I don't think the ecosystem will ever go back to using generative models for routing ever again.

q.t:
thoughts on Typesafe/Jev: I'm surprised that a general-purpose classifier (or discriminative model) can be just as interesting to the public as a general-purpose generative model. I've worked on search and discriminative models for years, so maybe I should have called this upfront, tbf I never thought about making them general-purpose beyond search. Typesafe also positions Jev really well as "System 1", a complement to the generative models we already have. Humble, unassuming, and sidestepping the frontier-lab warzone.

Jev's success could be disruptive to today's agentic systems in many ways, such as tool-calling and routing patterns. Over the last three years the consensus was to use a small generative model for routing, tool calling, MCP etc. Time to pause and rethink such architecture, because we'll probably see tool calling and routing move back to discriminative models. Whoever ships the next Jev-like open-weight base model will likely win the community.
